strengths: Timely identification of real DoS vulnerability in deployed MoE systems with clear practical implications for infrastructure providers
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 14 popular models and 139 HuggingFace models with multiple evaluation metrics (coverage, system-level latency, API latency)
Well-motivated theoretical framework: TMI formula correctly characterizes maximum imbalance with elegant regime analysis for sparse vs. dense models
Black-box attack requiring no gradient access or optimization, with model-agnostic applicability using simple repetitive token patterns
Novel side-channel finding that latency amplification patterns can infer backend model architecture and approximate deployment scale
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-defined threat model and methodology
Length scalability analysis (Fig. 6) demonstrates robustness across prompt lengths and system prompts, suggesting fundamental vulnerability rather than narrow edge case
weaknesses: Overstated universality claims: Abstract states 'nearly all models susceptible' but Table 3 shows significant variation (Mixtral 2.5-2.9× vs. Qwen3/GPT-OSS 1.01-1.35× at EP=8); sparser models exhibit substantially lower vulnerability, contradicting generality narrative

Shallow mechanistic understanding: Paper asserts embeddings are 'immediately dominated' by repetition but provides no ablation studies, dimension-wise analysis, or theoretical justification for why routers fail under repetitive inputs

Limited practical impact: Simple perplexity filtering (PPL~1 vs ~5) is highly effective and easily deployable; paper acknowledges no commercial APIs currently use it but doesn't evaluate robustness against mixed-pattern variants

Ethical concerns inadequately addressed: No clear evidence of responsible disclosure to affected service providers (ChatGPT, DeepSeek); side-channel architecture inference on commercial systems raises consent questions
Coverage metric (Eq. 4) measures theoretical concentration under worst-case GPU assignment but disconnects from actual latency; unclear how coverage of 0.6 maps to specific LAR values

Side-channel architecture inference claims are speculative: Inferring EP size from latency ratio lacks rigorous validation; other deployment factors (batching, dynamic reallocation, hardware heterogeneity) could produce similar latency patterns

Incomplete defense evaluation: Perplexity filtering tested only at extremes (PPL~1 vs ~5); Algorithm 1 evaluated via simulation only, not on deployed systems; no analysis of compatibility with existing load balancers (EPLB)
Limited technical novelty: Core attack is simply token repetition; the vulnerability is an artifact of EP architecture rather than a novel attack methodology requiring sophisticated design
Missing ablation studies: No analysis of partially repetitive tokens, sensitivity to different token patterns, or comparison with other input perturbations

Insufficient depth on router training: Does the auxiliary loss used in training inadvertently create the vulnerability? Could better-designed balance losses prevent imbalance under adversarial inputs?

strengths: Novel identification of routing imbalance as a weaponizable DoS vector in MoE systems; first work to demonstrate this threat distinct from prior resource exhaustion attacks

Comprehensive experimental validation across 139 MoE configurations with 13 representative models; thorough evaluation from multiple perspectives (cross-vocabulary, cross-model, latency impact, Expert-GPU mapping effects)
Strong theoretical foundation with clear mathematical characterization (Eq. 3-5) of embedding variance minimization objective and theoretical maximum imbalance bounds
Black-box attack requiring no knowledge of model parameters or routing mechanisms; practical demonstration on commercial LLM APIs showing 1.5-4.7× TTFT amplification
Real-world impact quantification including SLA violation analysis; demonstrates P99 degradation from 99% to 86.4% under realistic conditions
Transparent and honest discussion of practical limitations (Section 4.4, 5.4) including Expert-GPU mapping uncertainty and constraints on attack performance
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, well-organized research questions, high-quality figures (especially Figures 1, 3, 4), and accessible writing
Extended robustness analysis (Section 6.1) showing vulnerability persists across prompt lengths and system prompts; systemic nature of the architectural flaw
weaknesses: Critical gap between claimed universality and practical impact: Expert-GPU mapping is unknown in black-box settings, causing actual TTFT degradation to vary dramatically (1.22× to 2.48×) depending on unknown deployment details; Figure 3 demonstrates routing concentration doesn't guarantee GPU bottleneck

Theoretical-empirical connection incompletely justified: claim that token repetition solves the embedding variance minimization objective (Eq. 4) is empirically motivated but lacks formal proof of how layer-wise attention, position encoding, and normalization affect this assumption

Real-world DoS effectiveness underspecified: paper evaluates impact within batches or at low request rates (minute-wise for APIs) but doesn't quantify attack intensity (α) needed for SLA violations at operational request rates or total system throughput degradation at scale

Insufficient exploration of defenses: PPL-based filtering shows clear detection capability (Table 6: attack PPL ~1 vs natural text ~10-75) but dismissed as impractical without empirical overhead measurement; vulnerability-aware Expert placement achieves up to 36.7% reduction but dismissed too quickly

SLA analysis assumptions not fully validated: Log-Normal distribution parameters derived from aggregate request distributions; O(N) prefill complexity claim for Qwen3-30B-A3B needs broader validation; distribution shape parameter invariance claim needs clarification
KV caching bypass claim (Section 4.2) stated but not experimentally validated despite being presented as important to attack robustness

Reproducibility limitations: no code release announced; commercial API experiments irreproducible; vocabulary scanning process could be more precisely specified; some models have restricted availability
Responsible disclosure details missing: no specification of vendor contact, embargo periods, or specific mitigations recommended to system providers before public release
Missing ablation studies: which tokens are most effective? sensitivity to prompt structure? expected success rates given mapping uncertainty? detection difficulty measurements
